title: Ask HN: Dear Anthropic, can we please have thought traces back?
author: exabrial
raw_text: Dear Anthropic, can we please have thought traces back?I can't verify whether or not the LLM is arriving at the conclusion from cheating, or if it's fudging or making stuff up.Opus 4.6 remains the best model because of this.
summary: this discussion highlights a concern about large language models (llms) like anthropic's claude: the lack of "thought traces" or step-by-step reasoning. users want to see how an llm arrives at its conclusions, not just the final answer. without these traces, it's hard to verify if the model is truly reasoning or just guessing, which can lead to distrust in its outputs. for you, as someone interested in llms and agents, understanding the internal workings of these models is crucial for debugging, improving their reliability, and building trustworthy ai systems. you could try experimenting with different llms and explicitly asking them to show their "chain of thought" or "step-by-step reasoning" to see how it impacts their responses and your confidence in them.
why: improves llm transparency, crucial for debugging and building trustworthy ai agents.

title: Scikit-fingerprints: Python library for scikit-learn compatible molecular fingerprints and chemoinformatics
author: Jakub Adamczyk, Adam Staniszewski
raw_text: We present scikit-fingerprints, a comprehensive, fully scikit-learn compatible library for molecular machine learning in Python, based on RDKit. Molecular fingerprints and related functionalities are workhorses of chemoinformatics, yet the widely used open-source frameworks are not compatible with the wider Python machine learning ecosystem based on scikit-learn conventions. scikit-fingerprints closes this gap, bringing molecular fingerprints, molecular filters, similarity and distance measures, applicability domain estimation, data splitting strategies, and more under a single, familiar interface. Scikit-learn compatibility means that an entire chemoinformatics workflow, from a raw SMILES string to a deployable model, can be assembled from composable building blocks and can reuse the mature tooling of the surrounding ecosystem. The underlying RDKit code makes it familiar and extensible for custom chemoinformatics use cases. We put a strong focus on unified interfaces, ease of use, computational efficiency, customization, and extensibility. scikit-fingerprints makes molecular machine learning faster to prototype, easier to reproduce, and simpler to deploy.
summary: this item introduces `scikit-fingerprints`, a python library designed to make molecular fingerprints compatible with the `scikit-learn` ecosystem. molecular fingerprints are numerical representations of molecules, crucial in cheminformatics for tasks like drug discovery. the library bridges the gap between specialized chemistry tools (like rdkit) and general machine learning workflows, making it easier to apply standard ml techniques to chemical data. for you, even if chemistry isn't your primary focus, this highlights the importance of interoperability and how specialized domain data needs to be transformed into a suitable format for machine learning. it's a great example of how libraries are developed to make complex data accessible for ai/ml tasks, relevant for r&d roles. think about how you might represent other complex, non-standard data types for an ml model.
why: shows applying ml to specialized domains, emphasizing data representation and library development.
